The Curious Case of Reversible Elementary Second Order Cellular Automaton 115115

Enrico Formenti Email: enrico.formenti@univ-cotedazur.fr Affiliation: Université Côte d’Azur, CNRS, i3s
Nice, France Affiliation: Department of Computer Science and Engineering,
Birla Institute of Technology, Mesra, Ranchi, India    Supreeti Kamilya Email: supreeti.kamilya17@bitmesra.ac.in
Abstract

We prove that the reversible elementary second order cellular automaton rule 115115 is periodic when started on finite initial configurations. We also study some families of finite configurations that have interesting period functions.

1 Introduction

Cellular automata (CA) are a formal model widely used in the simulation of complex systems with application domains ranging from Biology to Mathematics and Computer Science.

CA can be seen as a collection of finite automata arranged on a regular grid. Each automaton updates its state on the basis of its own state and of the one of a fixed finite set of neighboring automata. All automata have the same transition function and update their state in parallel.

Higher order Cellular Automata (HOCA) have been introduced to include in the local rule time dependencies for modeling time dependent phenomena. The dynamical behavior of the class of CA is mostly still unexplored. Only a few results are known and they concern injectivity and surjectivity properties [3, 9]; or a specific subclass [6]. More recently, a systematic exploration of HOCA in which memory has been fixed to 22 (i.e. they remember their previous state) has started in [7]. From one end, one may remark that these systems can be seen as standard CA over a larger alphabet (see [6]) but adopting the larger alphabet hides all details about the micro-behavior which might be quite interesting in applications. From that preliminary explorations the authors came up with the class of reversible elementary second order CA (RESOCA) and more specifically on the one based on the elementary rule 115115. This has absolutely puzzling behavior which might result useful in practical applications. The main contribution of this paper is that all finite configurations have periodic behavior. However, the function which relates an initial (finite) configuration with its period seems to be quite complex and it is not fully understood yet. We show some families of initial configurations that have simple periodic functions and one which seems to have a quite complex periodic function with exponential growth with respect to the size of the initial configuration.

The paper is structured as follows. The next section introduces all the main notions used in this paper. Section 3 discusses the behavior of RESOCA 115115 and the many questions issued by it. The following section contains the proof of results in Section 3. The merge construction, one of the main tools used to generate new periods from finite configurations is briefly discussed in Section 5. Section 6 studies some families of initial (finite) configurations and their period. In the last section, we draw our conclusions and propose some perspectives.

Due to space constraints, most proofs and tables have been omitted. They will be included in the journal version of this work.

2 Preliminaries

2.1 Elementary Higher Order CA

An elementary higher order CA (EHOCA) consists of a tuple ⟨S,m,r,δ⟩\left\langle S,m,r,\delta\right\rangle where S={0,1}S=\left\{0,1\right\} is the set of states of the CA; m∈ℕm\in\mathbb{N} is the memory (also called the order); r∈ℕr\in\mathbb{N} is the radius and accounts for how many left and right neighbors are taken into consideration for updating the state of the current cell. Finally, δ:({0,1}2​r+1)m→({0,1})m\delta\colon\left(\left\{0,1\right\}^{2r+1}\right)^{m}\to\left(\left\{0,1\right\}\right)^{m} is the transition function (also called local rule) that updates the state of the current cell according to the content of the neighborhood and of the memory.

A local function δ\delta induces a global function Gδ:({0,1}ℤ)m→({0,1}ℤ)mG_{\delta}\colon\left(\left\{0,1\right\}^{\mathbb{Z}}\right)^{m}\to\left(\left\{0,1\right\}^{\mathbb{Z}}\right)^{m} that demonstrates the evolution of the current configuration in the next time step. An elementary second order CA sets the value of mm to 22. More precisely, for elementary second order CA, GδG_{\delta} associates the vector e→=(e1,e2)∈({0,1}ℤ)2\vec{e}=(e^{1},e^{2})\in\left(\left\{0,1\right\}^{\mathbb{Z}}\right)^{2} with the vector Gδ​(e→)∈({0,1}ℤ)2G_{\delta}\left(\vec{e}\right)\in\left(\left\{0,1\right\}^{\mathbb{Z}}\right)^{2} where Gδ​(e→)i1=ei2G_{\delta}\left(\vec{e}\right)^{1}_{i}=e^{2}_{i} and

Gδ​(e→)i2=δ⁡([(ei−11,ei1,ei+11)(ei−12,ei2,ei+12)])G_{\delta}\left(\vec{e}\right)^{2}_{i}=\delta\left(\begin{bmatrix}(e^{1}_{i-1},e^{1}_{i},e^{1}_{i+1})\\ (e^{2}_{i-1},e^{2}_{i},e^{2}_{i+1})\end{bmatrix}\right)

for all i∈ℤi\in\mathbb{Z}. In other words, the new vector at position ii is obtained by putting the old value of component 22 to component one, and computing the updated value of the new component 22 using the local rule δ\delta.

An EHOCA is injective if its global transition function GδG_{\delta} is one-to-one. If the function is onto, the EHOCA is surjective. An EHOCA is bijective if GδG_{\delta} is both one-one and onto. We recall that for any EHOCA, there exists a standard CA which is topologically conjugated to it [6]. Hence, we call a EHOCA reversible if and only if its conjugated CA is reversible. By a result in [8], the class of reversible EHOCA coincides with the class of bijective EHOCA.

The number of local rules of second order CA is quite huge. It goes beyond the scopes of this paper the dynamics all of them in a single paper. In this work, we propose to focus our attention on a special subclass of EHOCA rules δn′\delta_{n}^{\prime} that are induced by an elementary cellular automata rule δn\boldsymbol{\delta}_{\boldsymbol{n}}, more precisely :

δn′​([a,b,cd,e,f])=[eb+δn​(d,e,f)mod2]\delta^{\prime}_{n}\left(\begin{bmatrix}a,b,c\\ d,e,f\end{bmatrix}\right)=\begin{bmatrix}e\hfill\\ b+\delta_{n}(d,e,f)\mod 2\end{bmatrix} (1)

for all a,b,c,d,e,f∈{0,1}a,b,c,d,e,f\in\left\{0,1\right\}. We call this special class of second order elementary CA as RESOCA [7] defined by Equation (1).

A configuration is a function from ℤ\mathbb{Z} to {0,1}\left\{0,1\right\}. A configuration is finite iff only a finite number of cells have a state different from 00. For a finite configuration cc, define min⁡c=min⁡{i∈ℤ|ci=1}\min c=\min\left\{i\in\mathbb{Z}\;|\;c_{i}=1\right\} and max⁡c=max⁡{i∈ℤ|ci=1}\max c=\max\left\{i\in\mathbb{Z}\;|\;c_{i}=1\right\}. The length of cc is denoted |c||c| and is given by |c|=|max⁡c−min⁡c|+1|c|=|\max c-\min c|+1. A configuration c→=[bc]\vec{c}=\begin{bmatrix}b\\ c\end{bmatrix} is finite if both bb and cc are finite. For c→=[bc]\vec{c}=\begin{bmatrix}b\\ c\end{bmatrix} define min⁡c→=min⁡(min⁡b,min⁡c)\min\vec{c}=\min(\min b,\min c) and max⁡c→=max⁡(max⁡b,max⁡c)\max\vec{c}=\max(\max b,\max c), the length of c→\vec{c} is given by |c→|=|max⁡c→−min⁡c→|+1|\vec{c}|=|\max\vec{c}-\min\vec{c}|+1.

In this paper, we are going to make a large usage of some specific finite configurations for which we are going to introduce a specific notation. We denote 0¯\underline{0} a configuration in which all cells are in state 00; u¯\underline{u} a configuration in which all states are in state 00 except for the cell at position 00 that is in state 11.

2.2 Elementary Cellular Automata

An EHOCA is an elementary CA (or ECA) if memory m=1m=1. A cell of an elementary CA changes its state based on the states of itself, its left neighbor and its right neighbor. Hence, the local rule δ\delta can be conveniently represented in tabular form (see for example Table 1).

Interpreting the output row of the tabular representation of a local rule as a decimal number written in binary gives the well-known Wolfram’s number. Indeed, in the sequel of this paper we will refer to a specific ECA by its Wolfram’s number nn and refer to its local rule by δn\delta_{n}.

There are total 256256 distinct ECA rules. The rules exhibit different dynamical behaviour, from simple to chaotic. The ECA rules has been intensively investigated and several classifications of their dynamics have appeared over the years [2, 10, 5, 12, 4].

These 256256 rules are the basis for forming the second order CA rules studied in [7]. During the previously mentioned study we came across the rule 115115, which has a very curious behavior that motivated the present work.

3 The RESOCA 115115

Given a RESOCA ff, a configuration [mc]\begin{bmatrix}m\\ c\end{bmatrix} is periodic iff there exists an integer pp such that fp​([mc])=[mc]f^{p}\left(\begin{bmatrix}m\\ c\end{bmatrix}\right)=\begin{bmatrix}m\\ c\end{bmatrix}; the smallest pp satisfying the previous property is the period of [mc]\begin{bmatrix}m\\ c\end{bmatrix}. We say that pp is a period for RESOCA 115115 if there exists a finite configuration which has period pp for RESOCA 115115.

Theorem 1.

Any finite configuration is periodic for RESOCA 115.

The proof of the previous theorem is long and a bit tedious, and we leave it for the next section. The fact that RESOCA 115115 has a periodic behavior on finite configurations should not mislead us into thinking that the dynamics is very simple. None of this is true. We will see that there exist classes of configurations which present very complex sequences of periods, most of which are not yet fully understood. Let us start exploring some conditions that periods should satisfy.

Lemma 1.

For RESOCA 115, every periodic finite configuration has a period pp such that p≥3p\geq 3 and pp is a multiple of 33.

We call background the particular sequence of states that we can see in a column of the space time diagram of the configuration [0¯0¯]\begin{bmatrix}\underline{0}\\ \underline{0}\end{bmatrix} used in the proof of the previous lemma: [001001001001​…]T[001001001001\dots]^{T} (remark that all the columns are the same for this particular space-time diagram). Therefore, what the previous lemma says is that any finite configuration in a sense synchronizes his period according to the background, forcing it to be a multiple of 33. Hence, the following is a natural question.

Question 1.

For RESOCA 115115, in the context of finite configurations, are all multiple of 33 periods?

Remark that the product of two integers that are multiple of 33 is a multiple of 33. This means that if pp is a period, then p2p^{2} respects the necessary conditions given in Lemma 1. Hence, the question follows:

Question 2.

If pp is a period for RESOCA 115115, is p2p^{2} also a period?

We can not answer the previous question yet, but we can answer the following close version of it.

Proposition 1.

Consider two finite configurations of period pp and qq, respectively. Then lcm⁡(p,q)\lcm(p,q) is also a period.

The proof of the previous result is obtained via the merge construction that is explained in Section 5. In order to find arguments for answering to Question 1 we made several experiments which are reported in the following sections. All experiments were based on configurations of the type [u¯c]\begin{bmatrix}\underline{u}\\ c\end{bmatrix} where cc is a finite configuration. In this way, many periods were discovered : 3,6,12,15,27,30,54,60,63,123,…3,6,12,15,27,30,54,60,63,123,\ldots Two periods pp and qq are twins if q=p+3q=p+3. For example, in the previous sequence the periods 33 and 66 are twins as well as 1212 and 1515. We do not know whether all periods are twins, but twins seem to satisfy the following.

Conjecture 1.

Assume that pp and p+3p+3 are twins periods. Then, the next twins pair is p′p^{\prime} and p′+3p^{\prime}+3, where p′p^{\prime} is given by

p′=2​p+9−3​(−1)p2.p^{\prime}=2p+\frac{9-3(-1)^{p}}{2}\kern 5.0pt.

We cannot prove the conjecture but a weaker statement holds.

Proposition 2.

If pp and p+3p+3 are twin periods, then

p′={2​pif p is odd2​p+6otherwise.p^{\prime}=\begin{cases}2p&\text{if $p$ is odd}\\ 2p+6&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}

is also a period.

We remark that the previous proposition allows to produce a new period but not a pair of twin periods.

Finally, we observe that since all periods of RESOCA 115115 are multiples of 33 then, we can write Π=3​H\Pi=3H, where Π\Pi is the set of periods and HH is defined as follows

H={k∈ℕ| 3​k​ is a period of RESOCA 115}.H=\left\{k\in\mathbb{N}\;|\;3k\text{ is a period of RESOCA $115$}\right\}.

Hence, the initial question can be reformulated as follows.

Question 0*.

Is H=ℕH=\mathbb{N}?

If the answer to the previous question is negative then, more questions arise.

Question 3.

Is HH syndetic (i.e. does it have bounded gaps) or thick (i.e. does it contain arbitrary large intervals)?

Answering to these question is important not only for the theoretical aspects but also for the practical aspects like the application to cryptography that we propose at the end of this work, for example.

Proof of Theorem 1.

Consider two finite configurations bb and cc. If b=c=0¯b=c=\underline{0}, then it is not difficult to see that the space-time diagram of [0¯0¯]\begin{bmatrix}\underline{0}\\ \underline{0}\end{bmatrix} contains only background columns and hence has period 33. Now assume that at least one of bb or cc is different from 0¯\underline{0}. Without loss of generality we can assume that for all i<0i<0, ci=bi=0c_{i}=b_{i}=0 (otherwise we can choose c′=σu​(c)c^{\prime}=\sigma^{u}(c) and b′=σu​(b)b^{\prime}=\sigma^{u}(b), where u=min⁡[bc]u=\min\begin{bmatrix}b\\ c\end{bmatrix}). By Lemma 3, all columns with index larger than max⁡[bc]\max\begin{bmatrix}b\\ c\end{bmatrix} are background. We will distinguish three disjoint cases. For each of them, we will prove that for all i<−1i<-1, all columns in the space-time diagram of [bc]\begin{bmatrix}b\\ c\end{bmatrix} contain only background. This and the previous remark allow to deduce that the sequence of states that we can see in the space-time diagram of initial condition [bc]\begin{bmatrix}b\\ c\end{bmatrix} between cell −1-1 and cell max⁡[bc]\max\begin{bmatrix}b\\ c\end{bmatrix} is ultimately periodic. However, since RESOCA 115 is reversible, we can conclude that the sequence is periodic. Here are the proofs for the three cases announced above: 1) b0=0b_{0}=0 and c0=1c_{0}=1: this is Lemma 2; 2) b0=1b_{0}=1 and c0=0c_{0}=0: this is Lemma 5; 3) b0=1b_{0}=1 and c0=1c_{0}=1: this is Lemma 4. ∎

Another interesting consequence of the lemmata in this section is that, for any finite configuration c→\vec{c}, the size of the configuration and its position are essentially preserved along the evolution. More precisely, we can give the following.

Corollary 1.

Let ff be the global rule RESOCA 115115. For any finite configuration c→\vec{c}, we have ∀t∈ℕ​max⁡c→=max⁡ft​(c→)\forall t\in\mathbb{N}\;\max\vec{c}=\max f^{t}(\vec{c}) and ∀t∈ℕ∖{0}​min⁡f⁡(c→)=min⁡ft​(c→)\forall t\in\mathbb{N}\setminus\left\{0\right\}\;\min f(\vec{c})=\min f^{t}(\vec{c}). Moreover, min⁡f⁡(c→)−min⁡c→≤1\min f(\vec{c})-\min\vec{c}\leq 1.

Although the previous result follows rather directly from earlier results, it is nevertheless of significant importance. Indeed, a result of Moothathu implies that the existence of periodic points with the properties described in the corollary guaranties the existence of infinitely many periodic points with the same period [11]. Explicit examples of this fact are provided in Section 6.

5 The merge construction

We dedicate to this construction a separated section since it is useful in different situations when trying to build configurations with peculiar periods.

Consider two finite configurations c→1,c→2\vec{c}_{1},\vec{c}_{2}. By Theorem 1, these configurations are periodic of period pp and qq, respectively. Using Lemma 2 through 5, we remark that along the evolution of both configurations no modification (with respect to background) is made before min⁡c→1−1\min\vec{c}_{1}-1 (resp., min⁡c→2−1\min\vec{c}_{2}-1) or after max⁡c→1\max\vec{c}_{1} (resp., max⁡c→2\max\vec{c}_{2}). These facts suggest that if we build an initial configuration in which we position the non-background part of c→1\vec{c}_{1} on the left of the cell of index 00 and c→2\vec{c}_{2} on the right, leaving a sufficient number of cells in state 00 separating them, then we should have a new periodic configuration with the period which is some combination of the two original periods. More formally, define uu as the largest integer such that max⁡σu​(c→1)≤−3\max\sigma^{u}\left(\vec{c}_{1}\right)\leq-3 and vv as the least integer such that min⁡σv​(c→2)≥3\min\sigma^{v}\left(\vec{c}_{2}\right)\geq 3. Let us build a new finite configuration c→3\vec{c}_{3} that has a first component

∀i∈ℤ((c→3)1)i={σu​((c→1)1)iif ​i≤0σv​((c→2)1)iif ​i>0\forall i\in\mathbb{Z}\quad((\vec{c}_{3})_{1})_{i}=\begin{cases}\sigma^{u}((\vec{c}_{1})_{1})_{i}&\text{if }i\leq 0\\ \sigma^{v}((\vec{c}_{2})_{1})_{i}&\text{if }i>0\end{cases}

and as a second component

∀i∈ℤ((c→3)2)i={σu​((c→1)2)iif ​i≤0σv​((c→2)2)iif ​i>0.\forall i\in\mathbb{Z}\quad((\vec{c}_{3})_{2})_{i}=\begin{cases}\sigma^{u}((\vec{c}_{1})_{2})_{i}&\text{if }i\leq 0\\ \sigma^{v}((\vec{c}_{2})_{2})_{i}&\text{if }i>0.\end{cases}
Proposition 3.

Let c→1,c→2\vec{c}_{1},\vec{c}_{2} and c→3\vec{c}_{3} as above. Let pp (resp., qq) be the period of c→1\vec{c}_{1} (resp., c→2\vec{c}_{2}). Then, c→3\vec{c}_{3} is periodic of period lcm⁡(p,q)\lcm(p,q).

Proof.

The proof is trivial and left to the reader. ∎

Remark that the merge construction can be generalized, in the obvious way, to work with an arbitrary (but finite) number of finite configurations.

6 Families of configurations and their period functions

In this section, we focus our attention on families of initial configurations. Since all initial configurations share the same memory b=u¯b=\underline{u}, each family will be described solely in terms of its set of current configurations. Every family is defined by a regular expression depending on a parameter k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N}. For each value of kk, the corresponding regular expression generates a binary word ww of odd length, from which the current current configuration is constructed by setting c−k+i=wic_{-k+i}=w_{i} for i∈[0,|w|]i\in[0,|w|], where k=|w|−12k=\frac{|w|-1}{2}. Our objective is to determine the period function P⁡(k)P(k) associated with the family, that is, the function assigning the initial configuration of parameter kk its corresponding period.

6.1 Family 102​k−1​110^{2k-1}1 (k≥1k\geq 1)

This is a very simple family of configurations as it is confirmed by the following:

Proposition 4.

The period function P⁡(k)P(k) of the family 102​k−110^{2k-1}1 is as follows:

P⁡(k)={2 2​k+4−1,if ​k=1,215,otherwise.P(k)=\begin{cases}2^{\,2k+4}-1,&\text{if\ }k=1,2\\[4.0pt] 15,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}

6.2 Family 12​k+11^{2k+1}

Also this family of periods is pretty simple but we need a different proof technique than the previous one.

Proposition 5.

The period function P⁡(k)P(k) of the family 12​k+11^{2k+1} is as follows:

∀k∈ℕ,P⁡(k)={3if ​k=012if ​k=16otherwise.\forall k\in\mathbb{N},P(k)=\begin{cases}3&\text{if\ }k=0\\ 12&\text{if\ }k=1\\ 6&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}

6.3 Family 1​(01)k1(01)^{k}

For this family, the period function appears to be much more complex than the one of the two previous families. Using a computer program, we produced a long sequence of periods. However, we have no clue for a closed formula for the period function.

Looking more carefully, we remarked that P⁡(2​h+1)=42​h+3−1P(2h+1)=4^{2h+3}-1. We suspect that this is true for any h∈ℕh\in\mathbb{N}. Hence, we formulate the following.

Conjecture 2.

The period function P⁡(k)P(k) of the family 1​(01)k1(01)^{k} is such that P⁡(2​i+1)=42​i+3−1P(2i+1)=4^{2i+3}-1 for i∈ℕi\in\mathbb{N}.

For even values of kk, the period function P⁡(k)P(k) seems more complicate. However, from our experiments we could recognize a pattern. For i>2i>2, call qiq_{i} the number obtained by adding 11 to P⁡(2​i)P(2i) and then dividing the result by 88. We could remark that the representation in base 44 of qi=(P⁡(2​i)+1)/8q_{i}=(P(2i)+1)/8 is given by 1i​02​2i−2​31^{i}0^{2}2^{i-2}3 (the highest weight is at the left). Therefore, qiq_{i} can be written as qi=3⋅40+2⋅∑j=1i−24j+∑j=i+12​i4j=3+42​i+1−14⋅4i−1−83q_{i}=3\cdot 4^{0}+2\cdot\sum_{j=1}^{i-2}4^{j}+\sum_{j=i+1}^{2i}4^{j}=3+\frac{4^{2i+1}-14\cdot 4^{i-1}-8}{3}. Recalling the relation between qiq_{i} and pip_{i}, we get P⁡(2​i)=8​pi−1=23+2⋅42​i+2−7⋅4i+1−433=2⋅42​i+2−7⋅4i+1+53P(2i)=8p_{i}-1=23+\frac{2\cdot 4^{2i+2}-7\cdot 4^{i+1}-4^{3}}{3}=\frac{2\cdot 4^{2i+2}-7\cdot 4^{i+1}+5}{3}. We can therefore emit the following.

Conjecture 3.

The period function P⁡(k)P(k) of the family 1​(01)k1(01)^{k} is such that P⁡(2​i)=2⋅42​i+2−7⋅4i+1+53P(2i)=\frac{2\cdot 4^{2i+2}-7\cdot 4^{i+1}+5}{3} for i∈ℕi\in\mathbb{N}.

7 Conclusions and perspectives

In this paper, we investigated the behavior of RESOCA 115. In particular, we proved that, for every finite initial configuration, the evolution is periodic with period divisible by 3. We also identified families of finite configurations exhibiting either a simple period function or a considerably more intricate one. Nevertheless, the relationship between the structure of a finite initial configuration and the exact value of its period remains poorly understood. Clarifying this connection constitutes a challenging and promising direction for future research.

Through computational experiments, we identified the following periods: 3,6,9∗,12,15,27,30,54,60,63,123,126,135,189,246,252,255,270,315,378,507,510,615,630,1020,1023,1230,1260,1890,2043,2046,2535,25833,6,9^{*},12,15,27,30,54,\penalty 60,63,123,126,135,189,246,252,255,270,315,378,507,510,615,630,1020,1023,1230,1260,1890,\penalty 2043,2046,2535,2583 and many others. We emphasize that every period in this list arises from a finite configuration, with the notable exception of period 9. Indeed, rather curiously, we were only able to construct non-finite configurations exhibiting this period.

This observation prevents the use of the merge construction to fill the gap at period 1818. More precisely, the technique employed to establish the existence of period 99 does not extend to period 1818, as it would require the analysis of graphs with 2722^{72} vertices and 2742^{74} edges; far beyond the capabilities of our machines11 1 The technique used for period 99 was suggested by Jarkko Kari in a private communication.. Developing more efficient computational methods for proving or disproving the existence of a prescribed period therefore constitutes another compelling direction for future research.

All the hype surrounding the periods is that if we succeed in getting a certain amount of knowledge about them, then we could provide a concrete playground for a new secret sharing protocol in which the shares are given by some finite configurations and the secret is hidden in the period of a configuration obtained by the shares via the merge construction. We highlight several advantages of this new protocol. Suppose there are n shares, where nn itself is secret. In this setting, the presence of all shares is not necessarily required to decrypt the secret; however, one is not completely sure that the decryption is correct until every share has been taken into account. Moreover, the size of each share can be chosen to be logarithmic in the bit-size of its period, and the order in which the shares are processed is irrelevant.

A thorough analysis of this protocol is currently under investigation and will be presented in a separate forthcoming paper.
